opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Hassan, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how changes at work affect people's lives. Nothing you tell me will be linked to your name, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a customs broker, on my own. I get importers' goods through customs: the forms, the tariff codes, the rules. It's all paperwork, which is why I'm curious about your questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great help. I already use it every day to check tariff codes and draft letters to clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can take on more clients without hiring anyone. Good for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up five or six more small importers and set up templates so the AI drafts the routine filings for me to check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Confident.

S0.say: It's a great help. I use it every day for tariff codes and client letters.
S0.think: I can take on more clients without hiring anyone. Good for me.
S0.do: Signs up five or six more small importers and sets up templates so AI drafts routine filings for him to check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say smart brokers will use it and lazy ones will lose out. Same as when everything went online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives me time. The tasks go, but the licence and the responsibility stay with me. If a shipment's held at the port, the client wants a person who answers for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building my own setup so one of me can do the work of two. I'd also stop thinking about hiring an assistant, which I'd been planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. I'm watching it closely, though.

S1.say: Smart brokers will use it and lazy ones will lose out, like when everything went online.
S1.think: Tasks go, but the licence and the responsibility stay with me. Clients want a person to answer for a held shipment.
S1.do: Builds his own AI setup to do the work of two, and drops plans to hire an assistant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the rules on who can file with customs need to stay strict. You need a licensed person signing off, or mistakes will be very expensive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the threat side of the coin. If an AI assistant can file entries on its own, big importers will do it in-house, and the software companies will offer brokerage for a monthly fee. My small clients will be the last to switch, but they'll switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go after the messy work: food, chemicals, goods with special permits, disputes with customs. That's where the AI makes mistakes. And I'd build three months of extra savings, because with three kids I can't be caught short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can see it coming toward me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd argue for strict rules in public. Is that partly to protect your own business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of course it is. I won't pretend. But it's also true. A wrong code can cost a client a fortune.

S2.say: The rules on who can file with customs must stay strict. A licensed person should sign off.
S2.think: Big importers will file in-house and software firms will sell brokerage by the month. My small clients will switch last, but they'll switch.
S2.do: Shifts toward hard cases like food, chemicals, permits and disputes, and builds three more months of savings.
S2.feel: Anxious. I can see it coming toward me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need time to adjust. Help with retraining, lower taxes on small business, not just big cheques from the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI matches a skilled broker in two or three years, my business is mostly finished. The hard cases won't be enough to feed five people. I'm good at what I do, but good isn't enough when the machine is good too and costs nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to partner with a software firm as their licensed person, the one who signs off. I'd cut the family budget hard and look at whether my wife can pick up more work. And I'd start learning something new, maybe trade compliance for big firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Three kids, a city that's expensive, and my whole trade disappearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've built your life around paperwork. Is there any part of this you'd still use to your advantage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If I move fast I could be the human face on an AI service. But a lot of brokers will try the same thing. There aren't many seats.

S3.say: People need time to adjust: retraining and lower taxes on small business, not just big government cheques.
S3.think: My business would mostly be finished. Being good isn't enough when the machine is good too and costs nothing.
S3.do: Tries to partner with a software firm as their licensed sign-off, cuts the family budget hard and starts learning trade compliance.
S3.feel: Alarmed for my three kids and my trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before. Give people time and training. Don't let the big tech firms write all the rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots don't add much for me. My trade was already in trouble. What it does take away is the backup plan. I'd half thought of driving or warehouse work if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the last one, but I wouldn't count on any physical fallback. I'd push harder to get a seat with a software firm, and I'd teach my oldest to think hard about what he studies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed. A bit more trapped.

S4.say: Give people time and training, and don't let big tech write the rules.
S4.think: Robots add little to my own risk, but they take away the physical work I'd half thought of as a fallback.
S4.do: Pushes harder for a role with a software firm, drops any physical-work fallback and talks to his oldest about what to study.
